title: Ephemeral sessions get context via the curated shared tier, never raw memory
body: Raw transcript memory stays local by design (E2E-encrypted when synced between own machines) and is never shipped into ephemeral/web sandboxes: a private brain plus passphrase handling do not belong in a shared environment. The supported channel into ephemeral sessions and to teammates is this curated tier (.kit/shared/memory.jsonl) plus the repo CLAUDE.md. Closing the ephemeral-context gap therefore means feeding this tier at arc boundaries, not building new sync infrastructure.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: 6.3.2 is the release that MEASURES the attestation fix — docs stay caveated until it verifies
body: The GitHub artifact attestation errored in 327 ms on every kit release before 6.3.2 (subject-path dist/**/* = 1920 files vs the action's 1024-subject limit) and continue-on-error reported it to the jobs API as success. The fix packs the tarball and attests that single subject. Deliberate sequencing: docs/VERIFY.md keeps its caveat and the CI snippet keeps the attestation gate non-blocking (|| echo ::warning::) UNTIL gh attestation verify actually answers for 6.3.2. Removing them on the strength of an unrun fix is the exact failure the arc exists to correct — a check that could not run, reported as one that passed.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Prove a pinned CI secret from the run log, not by reading it
body: GitHub never exposes a secret's value, so 'is MAINTAINER_KEY_FPR the right fingerprint?' looks unanswerable from a workstation. It is not: the publish workflow's 'Import maintainer public key' step exits non-zero unless the imported key's fingerprint equals the secret exactly, and the imported key is the one committed at the verified tag. So a SUCCEEDING step plus the tag's own pubkey pins the secret's value transitively. Measured for 6.3.1 (run 30804371457): the log line reads 'Maintainer key fingerprint matches the pinned secret (single key in keyring)' and the pubkey at v6.3.1 is F6BBD5CDAFA615C51F43D73206EA76F88AC0482A. Generalise: when a gate compares a secret to something public and fails closed, a green run is a measurement of the secret.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A broken instruction can hide behind a true caveat — gate the command, not just the claim
body: docs/VERIFY.md shipped 'gh attestation verify --owner sandstream --repo kit <tarball>', which exits 1 (the flags are alternatives; --repo wants owner/repo). It survived review because the caveat directly above it truthfully said the attestation did not exist yet, so nobody expected the command to succeed. The caveat was accurate AND it camouflaged a defect in the same paragraph. Generalisation: when a doc hedges that something is unavailable, the instructions under that hedge stop being exercised — audit them at the moment the hedge is removed, and prefer an offline grammar gate over a fix. src/docs-verify-commands.test.ts does this for VERIFY.md/README/publish.yml; it deliberately avoids network so it cannot be skipped in CI, and asserts at least one invocation exists so deletion cannot make it vacuously green.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: The plugin policy channel carries the DECISION, not the config
body: kit-plugin-* packages must not import kit-core (adapter-sdk: monorepo coupling + private-package leaks), so [policy.agent_writes] cannot be enforced by a kit function call. Chosen: kit resolves every POLICY_OPS entry through the single policyDecision and exports only the refusals as KIT_POLICY_DENY (vendor:op, comma-separated). The plugin guard is then a membership test with NO rule in it. Rejected: serialising the config into the env and letting each plugin apply the four-state rule — that puts seven independent implementations of one access rule in seven packages, and each could collapse trap 1 (empty list = lock) or trap 2 (absent vendor != empty) on its own. Absence of the var must mean 'no denial', never 'denied', or every inert repo goes offline when a plugin runs outside a kit invocation. Two limits to keep stating: the channel is exactly as strong as KIT_READ_ONLY and no stronger, and a plugin-side refusal is NOT audited (a plugin has no path to the governed project's log).
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A fix inside packages/ does not ship until its package.json version is bumped
body: publish.yml's publish_ws skips any workspace whose version already exists on npm ('already on npm — skipping'). So a behaviour change in a kit-plugin-* package with an unchanged version lands in the monorepo and leaves every installed copy unchanged — silently, with a green publish run. This bit the containment fix for the plugin write surfaces: without bumping the seven touched plugins to 0.1.1, the read-only and policy guards would have existed only for people who cloned the repo. Treat a version bump as part of any packages/ fix, and remember the same shape as the pre-6.3.1 state where the scanner plugins existed but were unreachable to anyone who had not cloned.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A convention-enforced guard needs a test that derives the surfaces from source
body: kit-plugin-supabase shipped three write surfaces with no read-only guard while six sibling plugins had one, and four documents claimed 'every kit-plugin write surface' was covered. Nothing could catch it: the guard was a convention, and a convention is enforced by whoever remembers it. The gate that works (src/plugin-write-gates.test.ts) derives the surfaces from the plugin SOURCES rather than a maintained list — every function issuing a mutating request must appear in an expected mapping with both guards, in order, naming a registered op. Two details that matter: pin the MAPPING not just the presence (gating a token-revoke on env_set would satisfy a presence check), and add a second detector for writes routed through a shared transport (a GraphQL mutation's POST lives in the transport, so exempting the transport would exempt every future write through it). Exemptions carry written reasons and are asserted to still match something, so a rename cannot leave a stale grant behind.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A limitation recorded without its condition reads as permanent
body: The ROADMAP parked an upstream issue as unfileable: 'any repository outside the allowlist answers 403, so a human has to open it.' Measured when the item finally came up: gh issue list against that repo exits 0. The 403 was real but belonged to a DIFFERENT constraint — a cloud session's GitHub token is scoped to its one attached repo — and had been copied onto a local-session item where it never applied. Effect: an actionable item sat recorded as impossible, and the note was quoted forward through three session summaries without anyone re-testing it. Rule: when recording a blocker, record the CONDITION it depends on (which surface, which session type, which credential), and re-measure a one-line check before repeating the claim. A blocker without its condition is indistinguishable from a permanent one.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Drafted upstream issue dropped — the ask already existed, so evidence went to the open thread
body: ROADMAP carried a ready-to-file draft asking modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk to move its HTTP/OAuth deps to optionalDependencies. Searching upstream first found typescript-sdk#1924, open since 2026-04-17, asking the same thing with the same three options and two supporters. Filing the draft would have been a third +1. What was contributed instead: the measurement nobody in the thread had — which packages actually EXECUTE (9 of 94 load; all twelve HTTP/OAuth packages installed, none loaded), the method caveat (an ESM-only tracer misses ajv's internal require of fast-uri and under-reports by half), and the argument that beats disk footprint: of three advisories cleared from that subtree, two were unreachable and one (fast-uri via ajv) was genuinely live, and only a runtime trace tells them apart. Generalise: before filing a drafted issue, search the target repo — a duplicate spends the maintainer's attention and buries the thread that already has traction, whereas evidence added to the existing thread compounds. Prefer the measurement the thread lacks over restating its premise.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Never pipe a release gate's output through tail — the one run that matters is the one you then cannot read
body: Cutting 6.4.0, a full-suite run on the release branch reported '# fail 1'. The command was 'npm test 2>&1 | tail -8', so everything above the summary was discarded and the failing test's NAME was gone. Four subsequent full runs were green (4012/4012 each), so the flake could not be reproduced and remains unidentified. Cost: a known-flaky test in a release gate with no way to name it, which is exactly the shape that teaches people to re-run until green. Rule: capture a gate run to a FILE (npm test > run.log 2>&1) and read the summary from the file, so a failure keeps its detail. Related trap hit in the same session: 'cmd | tail; echo 0' reports tail's exit code, not cmd's — an attestation verify looked like it passed on an empty output until the exit code was read without the pipe. Both are the same error: putting a pipe between a measurement and its evidence.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A transitive-only vulnerability is fixed with overrides, not a new dependency
body: GHSA-8j4g-w8fx-2239 reached kit only through @modelcontextprotocol/sdk -> @hono/node-server (hono: ^4), and the SDK had no newer release to wait for. The fix was an overrides entry pinning hono 4.12.34, NOT a hono entry under dependencies: kit never imports hono, and declaring it would grow the stated runtime dependency surface in order to raise a range. Pick the patch-line version that still satisfies the consumer's range (4.12.34, not 4.13.0) so the override cannot silently widen what resolves.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Prove a raised timeout by making the test fail at the new number
body: A test that timed out at the SDK default (60s) was given a 150s harness default. The evidence that mattered was not the green run — it was putting the box under enough load that the same tests failed at exactly 150000ms instead of 60000ms. That number is what proves the new default is threaded through to the request layer rather than merely written down; a green run alone is consistent with the change having no effect. Corollary: when a per-request deadline is wall-clock and the work is a full repo scan, headroom over the MEASURED worst case is the requirement, and the raise must stay under the test runner's own --test-timeout so a genuine hang is still bounded.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Count what the repo can still prove, and fail closed on what it cannot
body: An append-only audit log is the right shape for a trail and the wrong shape for a counter. kit's bypass banner counted LINES in .kit-skipped-commits.jsonl, so three commits that a squash-merge had discarded were reported on every invocation — a warning that cannot go down is a warning nobody reads, and this was the only control making git commit --no-verify visible after the fact. The rule now: an entry is set aside only when it can be DISPROVED (the object resolves and no ref contains it); anything unverifiable — log carried between clones, object gc'd, not a repository — stays counted. Note the asymmetry: pruning needs proof, keeping does not. Two traps found while implementing: ask rev-list for '--all HEAD', because a detached HEAD is not a ref --all enumerates and a mid-rebase commit would read as orphaned; and state the set-aside count in the output rather than dropping it silently, or the fix becomes indistinguishable from the bug it replaced.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A wrapper that hands off to another wrapper must remove itself from the resolution path
body: kit's PATH shim resolved the real tool by skipping only its own directory. Another shim manager (mise/asdf/pyenv) applies the same rule and falls through to a PATH lookup when it has no version active for the cwd, so the two shims handed the call back and forth for hours without ever running the tool (#461). The rule that fixes it generalises: when handing off into another resolver, export a PATH with your own directory removed (every occurrence, trailing slash tolerated) rather than trusting a skip-my-own-dir rule the peer also has. A depth counter would have stopped the spin but still left the command unrun — for a control that promises 'never blocks', a hang is worse than no control.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Rewrite installed wrappers from the runtime path, not the install command
body: kit guard's shims are files written once by 'kit guard install'. Nobody re-runs an installer after upgrading the tool, so the #461 shim fix would have reached new installs only — a fixed kit sitting next to an old shim is still a hung machine. The self-heal now lives in 'kit guard-observe', the code path the shim itself invokes on every guarded command: if the calling shim's bytes differ from what the running version generates, it is rewritten. Two constraints came with it: the write must be a rename onto the path (sh reads a script while executing it, so a truncate-in-place splices the file under the running shim), and foreign files at a shim path are still never touched.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Keep personal agent capabilities out of repo config
body: Committed .kit.toml should declare project requirements only. Personal agent skills, web-search preferences, and other operator conveniences belong in the personal profile/defaults layer until kit has a governed source-agnostic skills pipeline and the repo intentionally declares a team-shared skill.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Classify secret findings by value, never by file path
body: kit's secrets gate splits trufflehog findings into buckets so the verdict can reach green. The 'example credential' bucket (unreachable host: loopback, bare compose/k8s service name, .internal, example.com; or placeholder secret: pass/password/changeme/a vendor doc sample) is keyed strictly on the finding's VALUE. Path-based suppression was rejected: a real credential pasted into a test file must still be flagged, and the degraded git-grep fallback only gets away with skipping test paths because trufflehog verifies live behind it. A verified-live finding is never waved through by any bucket.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: An accepted secret finding is scoped to one commit
body: .kit-secretsignore accepts a reviewed finding as <commit>:<file>:<detector>. Scope it to a single commit, never a path or regex: an entry must not be able to wave through a future occurrence of the same string. Verified-live findings stay unignorable regardless of the file. Prefer fixing forward over adding entries — derive fixture credentials at run time so nothing new accumulates in history.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Never commit a scanner-triggering literal to non-test source
body: A doc sample PAT held as a literal in src/ is a github-pat hit for the repo's own gitleaks job — correctly. Store such allowlist values as SHA-256 digests instead (recompute with printf %s '<token>' | shasum -a 256), and derive test fixtures that must LOOK live from a seeded hash at run time. Applies to any repo whose own CI scans its own history: the fixture that proves a scanner works must not itself become a permanent finding.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Rewriting public history to drop fixture literals — rejected
body: Considered rebasing d9f55af to drop three credential-shaped fixture literals and force-pushing main, which would leave zero suppression mechanism. Rejected: rewriting already-pushed history on a public repo risks divergence for anyone who fetched, and it buys nothing a commit-scoped .kit-secretsignore entry does not. The fingerprint-ignore path also gave every kit consumer the same escape hatch, which the rewrite would not have.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A generated value that is only plausible is worse than an absent one
body: kit init used to fill fields it could not prove: the operator's ~/.kit/defaults.toml services were appended to every project (a [services.posthog] block in repos with no PostHog), and the framework table supplied verify = "pnpm build" to npm repos. The rule now: generate only what the repo evidences, and report every declined field as a gap carrying the command that settles it (generateToml returns { toml, gaps }). An absent line is a question; a plausible line looks like a decision somebody made, so nobody re-reads it. known_services is a menu offered to whoever can answer, never a stamp.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: No-answer is null in promptMultiSelect, fallback in promptSelect — on purpose
body: The two interactive prompts deliberately disagree about what 'nobody answered' means. promptSelect answers with its recommended option (no TTY, Ctrl+D, closed input), which is what silently chose a secret backend on every agent and CI run. promptMultiSelect returns null instead, and the caller treats that as a gap, because no-answer must never become yes for something a repo does not evidence. Both routes now go through askQuestion, which reports no-answer once: Ctrl+D rejects the readline question with an AbortError, a closed input leaves it pending forever, so one is caught and the other is raced. Before that, Ctrl+D at the kit init services prompt ended the command on a node stack trace.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: tsconfig exclude for cloud-sync conflict copies — cannot work, gate instead
body: kit carried exclude globs (**/* [0-9].ts) meant to keep iCloud/Dropbox conflict copies out of the build. tsconfig globs support only *, ? and **/, never [0-9] character classes, so the pattern matched nothing and was fake protection. Excluding is also the wrong goal: the copy is gitignored junk that should be deleted, and hiding it from tsc is what made the class hard to diagnose (a type error at 'src/triage 2.ts:6', in code nobody wrote and no diff shows). Replaced by scripts/check-conflict-copies.mjs, which fails first in the build with the paths and the rm. It carries its own copy of the predicate because it runs before tsc; a test pins it to isSyncDuplicateName so the two cannot drift.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Tool output, not the tool schema, is what an agent loop pays for
body: Measured in kit-public with every scanner running: the standing MCP surface (tools/list) is 7,788 chars paid once per session, while one full kit_check response was 9,799 chars paid on EVERY call — and a check → fix → check loop calls it repeatedly. The response is now the verdict plus every non-passing row, with the complete run offloaded to .kit/runs/check-<stamp>.json and returned as detail.path (3,210 chars, 67% off per call; detail:true returns the full document inline). Two invariants bound the saving: only pass rows may be dropped (a skip or didNotRun always survives, because lost coverage is not a pass, and omitted passes stay counted), and scope is carried verbatim so a --category-narrowed green cannot read as a whole-repo green. A failed detail write returns no reference at all — a verbose answer beats a dangling pointer. scripts/measure-mcp-output.mjs reproduces both numbers.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: The dangerous moment moved from install to approval — gate the grant, never the review
body: npm skips a dependency's preinstall/install/postinstall/prepare unless package.json's allowScripts names it, so the moment that hands over arbitrary code execution is now the APPROVAL, not the install. install-gate matched install|i|add|ci|update and nothing else, so an agent could grant it unchecked. Both shipping spellings are gated (npm approve-scripts <pkg>, npm install-scripts approve <pkg>), --all/-a and the bare interactive form fail closed, and pnpm approve-builds too. The read-only faces are deliberately exempt: install-scripts ls/deny/prune, --dry-run and --allow-scripts-pending hand out nothing, and blocking the review step would push an agent straight to --all — a gate that makes review expensive buys the opposite of what it wants.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Measure the client, not the docs page, before parsing what a tool writes
body: docs.npmjs.com documents allowScripts as {pkg: "1.2.3"}. npm 11.19.0 writes the version into the KEY: {"esbuild@0.28.1": true} pinned, {"esbuild": true} unpinned (--no-allow-scripts-pin), {"esbuild": false} denied. The first parser followed the docs and was wrong in the field that decides pinned-vs-unpinned — the whole point of the check. The docs also list only npm approve-scripts while the client's own skip warning tells you to run npm install-scripts approve, so both spellings had to be gated. Rule: when a check parses a file some other tool writes, run that tool in a scratch fixture and read the result before writing the parser, and rewrite the tests against the measured shape rather than adapting the implementation to keep doc-derived tests green.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A release tag points at the commit its CHANGELOG describes, not at HEAD
body: publish.yml fires on a v* tag and builds the tag's tree, so the tag choice decides what npm gets. When feature PRs merge after the release-prep commit — 6.6.3 was prepared in #469, then #471 and #473 landed on main before anyone tagged — tagging HEAD would ship those features as the version whose CHANGELOG does not mention them. Tag the release-prep commit itself (v6.6.3 -> a3b6550) and let the later work wait for the next version. Verify after: npm view <pkg> version, plus install the published tarball and run its binary; the GitHub release should carry both SBOMs.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A gate's verdict must never come from a pipeline — GitHub's default step shell has no pipefail
body: GitHub Actions runs a bare 'run:' with 'bash -e {0}' — the -o pipefail flag is NOT set unless the step declares 'shell: bash' or sets it itself. So any condition of the form 'if ! check | tee log' takes its status from the LAST command, and tee always exits 0. kit's publish.yml carried exactly that around git verify-tag, so the tag-signature gate could not fail: an unsigned v6.6.4-predecessor (v6.6.3) published while the pinned MAINTAINER_KEY_FPR, the single-key keyring check and the ownertrust import were all correct and all unconsumed. Fix: 'set -o pipefail' plus a redirect instead of the pipe, and print the log only on failure. Enforced by self-audit R1-fail-open-ci (flags a condition piped into tee/cat unless the step really sets pipefail) — note the first version of that helper matched the word 'pipefail' anywhere in the step and was satisfied by the fixed step's own explanatory comment, so it now requires a real 'set' line. Applies to every repo: a green step that never evaluates its check is worse than no step.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A gate's verdict must never come from a pipeline — any status-blind sink, not just tee
body: Supersedes the tee/cat-only formulation. GitHub Actions runs a bare 'run:' with 'bash -e {0}' (confirmed in a runner log: 'shell: /usr/bin/bash -e {0}') — pipefail is NOT set unless the step asks. A condition whose pipeline ENDS in a status-blind sink is therefore decided by the sink: tee, cat, head, tail, wc, sort, uniq, tr. head and tail exit 0 on EMPTY input, which is the trap: 'if grep -rE pattern src/ | head -1' is always true. Two instances shipped in kit: publish.yml around git verify-tag (an unsigned v6.6.3 published) and security.yml around the security-headers grep (the warning branch was unreachable while the grep matched 0 lines). 'grep -q' as the last element is fine — there the pipe's last command IS the question. Enforced by self-audit R1-fail-open-ci. Two second-order lessons: widening the rule from the first instance immediately surfaced the second, so write the rule rather than patch the line; and the rule's pipefail-detection helper first matched the word anywhere in the step and was satisfied by the fixed step's own comment, so it requires a real 'set' line. Also: fixing such a check can turn it into a permanently-firing warning, which trains people to ignore warnings — gate it on the condition it presupposes (kit has no HTTP surface, so the header check now runs only when a server pattern exists) instead of shipping expected noise.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Removing the token IS the switch to OIDC — npm prefers a token whenever one is present
body: Configuring trusted publishers changes nothing on its own: npm authenticates with NODE_AUTH_TOKEN whenever that env exists, so OIDC only takes effect once the token is removed from the workflow. The two cannot both be in effect, which makes a re-added token a SILENT downgrade back to the credential npm is retiring (direct publishing by bypass-2FA tokens dies ~Jan 2027) — so gate it: a test that fails if any EXECUTING line of the publish workflow carries a token, comments excluded. Second-order facts from doing it on 13 packages: the per-package UI save requires step-up 2FA and npm does NOT keep the session elevated (one security-key tap per package, a timed-out prompt loses that save, nothing half-saves so retrying is free); the CLI equivalent 'npm access set mfa=publish <pkg>' returns EOTP and needs --otp from a TOTP app, which a security-key-only account cannot produce, and npm offers no way to add TOTP beside an existing key (only disable-and-re-enroll, a worse trade); driving the UI fast trips Cloudflare's bot check, which only a human may clear. And the honest limit of a prerelease smoke test: an unchanged workspace version is skipped as already-published, so per-package publishers stay UNEXERCISED until that package's next version bump — with no token fallback, a wrong field then fails that package's step and is fixed in the registry UI, not worked around.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A flag kit does not recognize must fail loudly, never fall through
body: hasFlag matches exact tokens, so a near-miss flag simply is not seen and the command silently takes a different branch: 'kit upgrade --self.' (trailing period) skipped the self-upgrade path and rewrote every installedAt in the lock file instead. Rule: any command that parses flags rejects unknown ones with exit 1 and prints its accepted set; command allowlists must include GLOBAL_FLAGS (--read-only/--readonly/--non-interactive/--env/--help/--version) so a documented global never reads as unknown. Globals may also precede the command word, so strip them before positional dispatch — command modules read subcommands off raw argv indices.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Scattered guards become a declared surface plus one refusal at dispatch
body: When a guarantee is enforced by N per-module guards, nothing can answer 'did we cover everything?' — read-only mode was guarded in 11 modules and four commands still wrote (identity init minted a private key), and flag validation covered 2 of 45 modules. The pattern that fixed both: enumerate the surface in a declared table (read-only-surface.ts, flag-surface.ts), enforce once at dispatch, and keep per-module guards as extras for library callers that bypass the CLI. Generate the table from the source and fail a drift test when it rots, because a table that falls behind REJECTS something that works — worse than the silence it replaced. An allowlist authored from the handler file alone is the known trap: CHECK_FLAGS rejected kit check --attest, documented and read one import away.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A coverage oracle must measure the property, not the shape of the fix
body: self-audit's flag-validation row grepped src/commands/*.ts for the string unknownFlags(, which measured whether a file contained a guard: a module with several handlers could hold one and leave its other verbs open, and the verbs fix and plugin do not live under src/commands at all, so no grep there could ever see them. Rewritten to 'every verb in COMMAND_REGISTRY has an entry in the declared surface'. Same trap as trap 5 (a correct decision function with no caller is not a working control) and as #470, where the anchor record was correct, complete, 0600 and read by nothing. When changing an oracle to make a rule pass, the new oracle has to be strictly stronger — and a missing table must report every verb as missing, never as covered.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Report a fact and you must assert it, or mark the output as possibly partial
body: kit makes three kinds of statement — measurement (vercel 53.1.1), assertion (matches what the repo declared), verdict (green) — and the defect class is a verdict that refers to something other than the measurement while the reader takes them as the same. Measured instances: a latest pin printed the installed version while green meant 'the binary answered --version'; cli-lock.json recorded a guessed installer while green meant 'a key with that name exists'; identity was printed with NO verdict, which forces the reader to supply one, and an agent always does. Two branches, both required: if the fact can be compared to a declaration, compare it (git.email and gcloud.account already did; vercel.user did not — that was the whole gap); if it cannot, label the output unknown or skip WITH THE REASON, never green. Unknown is not failure — unknown must be visible, and kit already has the vocabulary. Generalises to anything whose COMPLETENESS depends on the caller's authority or on a lookup that may not have run: a scanner without a token, a registry offline, a listing filtered by a role, and a verdict whose oracle can only see one working tree.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A gate never calls the network: it reads a cache and says when the cache is cold
body: Resolution of a real conflict between two of kit's own rules — no false green (verify against the registry) versus the gate must stay fast and offline-safe (do not call out). A gate that makes network calls becomes slow, flaky, skipped, and false-green the moment a call fails and the code shrugs. The design: split who FILLS the cache from who READS it. An explicit user-initiated command fills it (kit tools list --latest, ~12s cold); the gate reads only, reports drift it already knows, and otherwise prints 'not looked up yet — run <the filling command>'. Two details carry the honesty: a failed lookup is NOT cached, or a flaky network becomes a day-long policy; and air-gap gets a different reason string from cache-cold, because 'we did not call' and 'we have not looked yet' are different facts for the reader. The next verification that wants to live in a gate answers three questions instead of one: who fills, who reads, and what do we say when it is cold.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Counting activity proves a gate existed, not that it still works
body: kit usage counts what kit recorded — refusals, coverage, triage. That is evidence of activity, not evidence the floor works: a gate can be installed, counted, and broken. So --prove runs live negative controls (an unverifiable install must be blocked, a staged credential must fail git commit) in a throwaway dir, offline. Each refusal control is paired with a must-allow control, because a gate that refuses everything would pass the refusal test while being an outage. A control that cannot be set up reports inconclusive with its reason, never a pass it did not observe.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: No token-savings number: there is no counterfactual to divide by
body: kit usage deliberately reports no 'saved you N tokens' or money figure. There is no counterfactual for what the same work would have cost without kit, and a savings number without one is invented — the same rule that makes a check report what it could not run. What is measurable is the reliability axis: the size of the enumerated set, how much of it could not run and why, and whether two runs agree. The could-not-run rows are the product as much as the passing ones.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Automated pty test via script(1) — rejected, it hangs CI
body: Tried to gate the interactive view (alternate screen, tab switching, restore on exit) with an automated test that gets a pty from script(1). Rejected: script hangs when its own stdin is not a terminal (spawnSync with an input pipe gives a socket, and tcgetattr fails), so the test hangs the job instead of gating it — one attempt did exactly that locally. Verified by hand through a pty instead, and the test file records what was verified and why the automated version was dropped. Also: pgrep -f 'cli.js usage' matches script's own argv, so signalling the wrong process makes a working restore look broken.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Do not regenerate src/flag-surface.ts casually — the drift test only checks one direction
body: scripts/derive-command-flags.mjs --emit currently rewrites ~512 lines, narrowing the accepted-flag sets of 70+ existing verbs versus the committed artefact. The drift test asserts only the subset direction (every flag the code reads must appear in the table), so a narrower generated file still passes and the committed artefact can rot without failing CI. Adding a new verb: hand-add its row instead of regenerating, or take the regeneration as its own change with its own reasoning — it alters flag validation for every command.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A new security check needs its exclusion list measured, or it gets switched off
body: Every check added to kit check must be tried against the repos it will actually run in before it ships, and the false-positive cases documented with the measurement. Two from one day: scanning kit's own dist/ for bundle credentials produced 73 hits, every one a test fixture or one of kit's own detection patterns — a check that fails on the repo shipping it is a check nobody keeps. And a name check on client-exposed env vars must excuse ANON_KEY / PUBLISHABLE_KEY / SITE_KEY / DSN / CLIENT_ID: those are the most common client env vars there are and they are meant to be public. A check that fires on day one is disabled before it ever catches the real leak, so the exclusion list is part of the feature, not a follow-up. Corollary: the passing cases deserve tests as much as the failing ones.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: kit is one layer, not the stack — nothing may assume a harness or a UI framework
body: The developer chooses the interface: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or the next one. kit sits underneath as a governance layer and must work identically under all of them, so no check, command or output may branch on which harness is in use. Two consequences. First, UI-level gates (button naming, dead click handlers, framework-specific lint) belong in the project that has the UI, not in kit — a JSX-aware check would fail on every project not built like the one it came from, which is how a check gets switched off. Second, when kit borrows a look — kit usage uses a boxed tabbed layout resembling Claude Code's /usage because that is the terminal the operator was in — the layout is a reference, never a dependency: the data comes from kit's own records and the harness appears only as a value in a column (measured: claude-code and codex sessions read through identical code). Anything that would need a specific harness installed to work belongs above kit's layer.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Regenerating flag-surface.ts is safe — the earlier warning was a misread formatting diff
body: Reverses 0ef8d4, which claimed that scripts/derive-command-flags.mjs --emit narrows the accepted-flag sets of 70+ verbs. It does not. Measured properly: the derived surface and the committed table agree on all 72 verbs, zero content differences. What the 512-line diff actually was: emit() wrote one verb per line while Prettier wants one flag per line, so a no-op regeneration reflowed the whole file. The lesson worth keeping is about method, not about flags — a line-count diff is not evidence of content change, and I reported a defect from git diff --stat without parsing either side. Fixed by making emit() produce Prettier's shape so regeneration is byte-identical, plus a test that compares the generated string to the committed file and points at the first differing line. A generated file nobody dares regenerate is a hardcoded table wearing a generator's hat.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: The decision ledger gates shape, never content
body: kit requires a per-run decision ledger (.kit/decisions.jsonl) and schema-checks each entry — the decision, a confidence, what was assumed, and the question it would have asked had asking been free. It deliberately never scores the content. Writing the entries is model work the zero-LLM core does not do, and a gate that reads the reasoning makes the ledger get written for the gate, which is the incentive the auditor separation exists to remove. Absent/empty under [decisions] require = true is didNotRun; a malformed entry is a plain fail so --lenient cannot wave a corrupt ledger through as an unavailable scanner. Same line kit standards and the advisory baseline already hold.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: kit's own repo does not require a decision ledger
body: [decisions] require = true is deliberately NOT set in kit's own .kit.toml. The ledger is a per-run artifact produced by an agent-governed run; on a plain CI checkout no agent ran, so requiring one there would gate on the absence of something nothing was asked to produce. require = true belongs on agent-governed runs, not on every checkout. Revisit if kit's CI ever runs an agent that records decisions.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A config section is declared in three places, and the third one warns
body: Adding a .kit.toml section means kitConfig (type), CONFIG_SECTIONS (config-surface.ts, generates docs/CONFIGURATION.md) AND KNOWN_SECTIONS (config.ts), which loadConfig warns from. The first two were pinned to each other; the third had drifted by two — [supply_chain] and [coverage] are real, honoured sections that printed 'unknown section … (likely a typo)' on every kit invocation. A warning that fires on correct configuration trains the operator to ignore the one that fires on a real typo. config-surface.test.ts now pins all three in both directions.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A gate that exists but is never invoked is the default failure, not the exception
body: kit adopted its own ADR gate in #403 and no workflow, hook or agent instruction ever called it — armed and unfired for a month, while the rules provably caught violations. A gate nobody runs emits nothing, and nothing reads exactly like a clean run. self-audit-ci already proves every script a workflow points AT exists; the inverse (a gate that exists is pointed at by something) had no rule. When adding a gate to this repo, wire the invocation AND pin it with a test that strips comments and forbids continue-on-error / || true — a gate named in a comment is not a gate, and one that cannot fail the build is a report. General case tracked in #533.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: pre-commit excludes full npm test until suite timeouts are fixed
body: kit-public uses externally managed .githooks. [hooks].pre-commit should require staged security scan + build, not full npm test: a real pre-commit run on 2026-08-27 hit Node test file timeouts in dist/policy-gate.test.js and dist/secrets-propagate.test.js. Re-add full npm test only after those suite timeouts are fixed or the suite is split for hook use.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>
